description.text: In October 1815 a thickset man of forty-six or forty-eight walks into Digne an hour before sunset: shaved head, long beard, a yellow shirt, a new soldier's knapsack, a huge knotted stick and iron-shod shoes on bare feet. He has money and will pay, but both inns, the prison, a peasant's cottage and even a dog's kennel turn him out. An old woman points him to the little house beside the Bishop's palace.

He tells the Bishop everything at once: his name is Jean Valjean, he left the galleys of Toulon four days ago after nineteen years, and his yellow passport says 'very dangerous man'. He is stunned to be called 'monsieur', fed off silver by candlelight and given a bed with white sheets, and never once reminded of what he is.

Hugo tells his story. A peasant of Brie who never learned to read, he was raised by an older sister and, when her husband died, fed her seven children by pruning trees at Faverolles. In the hard winter of 1795 he broke a baker's window and took a loaf. Five years in the galleys became nineteen through four attempts at escape; at Toulon he was number 24,601. He never heard of his sister's family again.

The galleys made him his own judge. He admitted his theft, then condemned society for the weight of the punishment and Providence for making society, and learned to read at forty to sharpen his hatred. He is the strongest man in the hulks, 'Jean the Jackscrew', and can climb the angle of a wall like a cat. He has not shed a tear in nineteen years.

Freed, he was handed a hundred and nine francs for nineteen years' work and paid half wages at Grasse as an ex-convict. In the Bishop's alcove he cannot sleep for thinking of the silver. At two in the morning he takes off his shoes, stands over the sleeping old man with an iron candlestick in his fist, halted by the serene face in the moonlight, then takes the basket of silver and goes over the garden wall.

Gendarmes bring him back at dawn. The Bishop says the silver was a gift, hands him the two silver candlesticks as well, and tells him quietly that he has promised to become an honest man: 'It is your soul that I buy from you.' Valjean, who promised nothing, cannot answer.

Wandering the fields in turmoil, he sets his foot on a forty-sou piece dropped by a little Savoyard and drives the boy off. Then he sees what he has done, runs calling for the child across the darkening plain, and weeps for the first time in nineteen years. Hugo says he must now rise higher than the Bishop or fall lower than the convict. That night a carter sees a man kneeling in prayer before the Bishop's door.

The narrator says it outright: M. Madeleine is Jean Valjean. After Digne he sold the silver but kept the candlesticks, crossed France, and built the prosperity of Montreuil-sur-Mer under a new name, living by two rules, to hide his name and to sanctify his life. Javert's news, that an old man called Champmathieu is about to be condemned as Jean Valjean, opens a night-long battle: stay Madeleine and go on doing good for a whole town, for Fantine and her child, or give himself up and save an innocent stranger. He burns the clothes he wore into Digne and the forty-sou piece, nearly melts the candlesticks, hears his own name cried within him, and ends the night undecided.

He sets off for Arras without having decided anything. A wrecked wheel at Hesdin feels like Providence stopping him, but he hires an old woman's rickety cart and presses on over bad roads, and reaches the courthouse at eight at night. He sends in his card as the Mayor of Montreuil-sur-Mer.

Hidden behind the judges, he watches an old wheelwright who looks like himself as he was in 1815, and hears three ex-convicts swear that this is Jean Valjean. Then he stands up, his hair turned white in an hour, and tells the court to release the prisoner: he is Jean Valjean. He proves it by reminding each convict of a private mark from Toulon, and walks out with no one daring to stop him. Champmathieu is freed.

Back at dawn, he is at Fantine's bedside when Javert arrives with a warrant. Javert takes him by the collar and refuses him three days to fetch Cosette, and Fantine dies on learning that her child was never brought. Valjean wrenches an iron bar from a bedstead to keep Javert off, lays the dead woman out with a mother's care, whispers something in her ear that no one hears, and gives himself up.

He breaks out of the town jail that night, slips back to his room, labels the cudgel tips and the forty-sou piece for the court, leaves his money for Fantine's funeral and the poor, and wraps up the Bishop's candlesticks. Sister Simplice's lie sends Javert away, and he vanishes on foot toward Paris. The town that blessed him has turned on him within hours.

Newspapers of July 1823 report that he was retaken in Paris boarding a coach for Montfermeil, after withdrawing more than half a million francs from Laffitte's bank, which has not been found. Tried at the Var Assizes for robbing Petit-Gervais, he refused to defend himself, was condemned to death, and had the sentence commuted to the galleys for life. At Toulon he is now number 9,430. Montreuil-sur-Mer's prosperity dies without him.

In late October 1823 a white-haired life convict breaks his ankle chain with one hammer blow, climbs the rigging of the warship Orion and saves a sailor dangling from a yard, while the crowd on the quay cries for his pardon. Coming down, he falls into the sea between two ships and never surfaces. The Toulon paper reports convict 9,430, Jean Valjean, drowned.

Jean Valjean was not dead. He had let himself fall, swum underwater to a moored boat and escaped by a mole's track across France to Paris, where he read of his own drowning. He bought mourning clothes for a little girl and went to Montfermeil: he was the stranger in the yellow coat who carried Cosette's bucket, gave her the doll and paid fifteen hundred francs for her. Now he carries her into Paris asleep on his back.

In fifty-five years he has never been father, lover, husband or friend, and all his dammed-up affection rushes to the child. In a garret of the Gorbeau house on the Boulevard de l'Hôpital he teaches her to read, talks to her of her mother and makes her pray, and she calls him 'father'. The Bishop brought him the dawn of virtue, Hugo says; Cosette brings the dawn of love.

He goes out only at dusk, in his yellow coat, and the neighbourhood calls him 'the beggar who gives alms'. The prying old portress watches him take a thousand-franc note from the lining of his coat, and finds wigs in his pockets.

Glimpsing Javert under a beggar's rags, and then from behind as a new lodger listening at his door, he gathers his money and leaves with Cosette at nightfall. Javert and his men follow through the Mouffetard quarter and over the Pont d'Austerlitz into the lanes of the Petit-Picpus, where a blind alley and a sentinel close both ways out.
With a patrol coming up the street, he cuts down a lantern rope, climbs a sheer wall with his old convict's skill, hauls Cosette up after him and drops with her into a vast, silent garden.

The man with the bell on his knee greets him as 'Father Madeleine': it is old Fauchelevent, whom he once lifted from under a cart and placed here as gardener. The house is the convent of the Petit-Picpus, where no man may enter, and Fauchelevent hides the two of them in his hut.

To come in by the front door he must first get out. He has himself nailed into the empty coffin meant for a dead nun, is carried to the Vaugirard cemetery and lowered into the grave, and faints as earth falls on the lid. Fauchelevent gets him out in time.
The prioress admits him as Ultime Fauchelevent, the gardener's brother, and Cosette as a charity pupil.

He gardens beside Fauchelevent, never goes out, and sees Cosette for an hour a day. Comparing the convent with the galleys, he is humbled: the convicts expiated their own crimes, these innocent women expiate other people's. He prays at dusk outside the chapel window, and reflects that two houses of God took him in at the two crises of his life. Years pass.

Thénardier's shouts settle it for the reader: the white-haired gentleman Marius has watched at the Luxembourg is the man in the yellow coat who carried off the Lark on Christmas Eve 1823, Jean Valjean, and his daughter is Cosette. Trapped in the Gorbeau garret, he denies knowing Thénardier, gives his name as Urbain Fabre and a false address to gain time, cuts his ropes with a convict's hidden saw, and lays the red-hot chisel on his own bare arm to show that pain will not make him speak. He has not once cried out: a man who wants no police.
While Javert is busy with the gang, he slips out of the window and down the rope ladder. Marius still does not know who he is.

The narrator now says where he has been. In 1829, after five hidden years, he left the convent because Cosette was being drawn toward the veil and he would not choose that for her. As M. Fauchelevent he rents a secret house in the Rue Plumet with a hidden passage to the Rue de Babylone, and keeps two other lodgings, in the Rue de l'Ouest and the Rue de l'Homme Armé, so as never again to be caught unprepared.

Cosette has the pavilion and every comfort; he sleeps in a bare lodge in the back courtyard, without a fire, and eats black bread. They walk in the Luxembourg, give alms at Saint-Jacques-du-Haut-Pas and visit the poor. As M. Fauchelevent he even mounts guard in the National Guard, glad of a uniform that makes him look like any other taxpayer.
He explains everything to Cosette from his reading and his suffering, and answers every question but one: he will not tell her her mother's name.

He noticed the young man at the Luxembourg before Cosette betrayed anything, set little traps for him and came to hate him. When the youth followed them home and questioned the porter, he moved house and gave up the Luxembourg for good.
One October dawn at the Barrière du Maine he and Cosette watch the chain-gang pass on its way to the galleys. He is petrified; she asks whether those are still men.
The burn on his arm from the Jondrette garret keeps him in bed for a month. Cosette nurses him, their old closeness comes back, and he blesses the wound.

He has seen Thénardier prowling the quarter and found an address freshly scratched on his garden wall, and resolves to take Cosette to England. On the Champ-de-Mars a paper drops on his knees: 'Move away from your house.'

He moves Cosette and Toussaint to the Rue de l'Homme Armé, carrying only the little valise Cosette calls his 'inseparable'. There, in a mirror, he reads backwards the blotted imprint of her note to her lover. The light of his life goes out; he guesses the young man of the Luxembourg and finds hatred in his heart.

A street boy hands him Marius's farewell letter to Cosette. He reads 'I die' with a frightful inward joy: his rival is going to his death of his own accord, and he need only keep silent. Then he grows gloomy, and an hour later goes out in full National Guard uniform with a loaded gun, toward the fighting.

He enters the barricade unannounced and throws down his uniform so that a fifth father of a family can escape. Marius recognises M. Fauchelevent; Javert, bound in the taproom, recognises Jean Valjean.

He fights without killing. He shoots through the ropes of a mattress hanging in a distant window and walks out under fire to fetch it as a shield against grapeshot, and knocks the helmets off two spies on a roof instead of shooting them.
He asks Enjolras, as his only reward, for the right to shoot Javert. In the lane behind the barricade he cuts Javert's cords, tells him his name and address, sends him away, and fires into the air.
In the final assault he catches Marius as he falls wounded, carries him into a sheltered corner, finds a grating under the paving-stones and goes down with him into the sewers of Paris.

Through the long underground hours he slips past a police patrol, binds Marius's wounds with his own shirt, finds the grandfather's address in his pocketbook, and wades into a fontis of liquid mud until only his head is above it, holding Marius up, before his foot finds solid stone and he kneels to pray.

At the river outlet the grating is locked. A man with a key appears: Thénardier, who does not know him under the mud, takes him for a murderer getting rid of a body, takes his thirty francs and lets him out.

Javert is waiting on the shore. Valjean gives his name and asks only to take Marius home first. Javert drives them to the Rue des Filles-du-Calvaire and then, at his asking, to his own door, and tells him to go up. When Valjean looks out from the landing, the street is empty.
Months later, as M. Fauchelevent, he brings Cosette to the convalescent Marius and lays six hundred thousand francs on the table as her dowry.

The money is M. Madeleine's, withdrawn from Laffitte in 1823 and buried with the Bishop's candlesticks in a glade of the Montfermeil forest; he has just dug it up under Boulatruelle's nose. He has also read in the Moniteur that Javert drowned himself.

He gives Cosette a legal identity as the orphan Euphrasie Fauchelevent, heiress to an anonymous legacy, and denies to Marius that he ever set foot in the Rue de la Chanvrerie. When Marius swears he would give all Cosette's fortune to find the man who carried him through the sewers, he says nothing.
Pleading a crushed thumb, he wears his arm in a sling so that he cannot sign the marriage papers, lets M. Gillenormand give Cosette away, and slips out of the wedding feast.
In the empty flat he opens the 'inseparable', lays out the little mourning clothes Cosette wore leaving Montfermeil, and weeps over them, wrestling all night with his conscience for the last time.

The next morning he shows Marius his unhurt thumb and tells him the truth: he is Jean Valjean, an ex-convict and a fugitive, a peasant of Faverolles, nothing to Cosette but a passer-by who took in an orphan. He confesses because a name stolen to live would be a lie lived every day. He asks only to see her sometimes, and Marius coldly allows him the evenings.
He comes each evening to a damp room on the ground floor, refuses Cosette's kisses, calls her 'Madame' and makes her call him 'Monsieur Jean', slowly detaching her from himself.
When first the fire and then the armchairs disappear from the lower room, he understands that he is being shown the door, and stops coming.
Every evening he walks toward Cosette's street, peers round the corner weeping and turns back, each walk a little shorter than the last.
He takes to his bed and stops eating. The doctor tells his portress that he is dying of having lost someone dear to him.

In his old workman's clothes, with Cosette's little dress laid out and the Bishop's candlesticks lit in daylight, he starts a letter telling her that her fortune was honestly earned, and breaks off sobbing that he will die without seeing her again.

Cosette and Marius come, knowing at last what he did. He asks their pardon, tells them her money is honest, leaves her the candlesticks, asks for a grave with no name, tells her that her mother was called Fantine, and dies with his hands on their heads. Hugo thinks it likely the Bishop was there.
He lies under an unmarked stone in a lost corner of Père-Lachaise. Four lines someone once pencilled on it have been washed away by the rain.

description.text: Fantine's child by Tholomyès, a pretty little girl decked in all her mother's finery; her real name is Euphrasie. When Fantine, walking home to Montreuil-sur-Mer, sees the innkeeper's two little girls on a swing at Montfermeil, she leaves Cosette with their mother for seven francs a month, paid six months in advance, and goes on weeping.

Her wardrobe pawned, she is dressed in rags and fed from a wooden bowl under the table with the dog and cat. Madame Thénardier beats her, and her daughters copy her. Before she is five Cosette sweeps, carries and runs errands; before six she sweeps the street in the dark of winter mornings. Only her big sad eyes are left of the rosy child, and the village calls her the Lark: small, trembling, up before anyone, and never singing.
Thénardier's lies about her, that she is naked in the cold and then dying of a fever, cost her mother her hair and her front teeth.
The mayor of Montreuil-sur-Mer, who has taken in her dying mother, sends three hundred francs and then three hundred more to bring her. Thénardier, scenting money, invents bills and keeps her.
Her mother dies at Montreuil-sur-Mer without having seen her again.

Christmas Eve 1823. She is eight, kept as an unpaid servant since her mother's money stopped, with a black eye from a blow, knitting under the table while carters drink. Her one terror is to be sent at night to the spring in the forest. Caught in a lie about the peddler's horse, she is sent, with a bucket bigger than herself and a fifteen-sou piece for bread.
Bucket in hand, she stands spellbound before the toy stall opposite the inn and its magnificent doll in pink crepe, 'the lady', until Madame Thénardier's voice sends her running.

Alone in the black forest she fills the bucket, losing the coin in the spring without knowing it, and staggers back crying 'O my God!' Then a huge hand silently lifts the weight. A man is walking beside her, and she is not afraid.

The stranger saves her from the whip, buys the stockings she is knitting so that she may play, and when she is caught nursing the Thénardier girls' cast-off doll, goes out and brings back the great doll from the stall. She names it Catherine. In the night he slips a gold louis into the wooden shoe she has set on the hearth.
At dawn he pays fifteen hundred francs for her, dresses her in the mourning clothes from his bundle, and walks her out of Montfermeil by the hand.
The stranger is Jean Valjean. After a strange day of carriages and hedgerow meals she falls asleep on his back, still holding Catherine, as he carries her into Paris.

She wakes in a garret of the Gorbeau house expecting to be set to work and is told to play. She sings from daybreak, learns to read, prays for her mother, and calls the kind man 'father', knowing no other name for him. A child no one ever let love anything, she loves him with her whole being.
Hunted with him through the night streets, she is tied to a lantern rope, hauled up a wall and dropped into a dark garden, where she comes close to freezing.
The prioress of the Petit-Picpus admits her as the granddaughter of Ultime Fauchelevent, a charity pupil whom she expects to 'grow up ugly'.

She keeps silent, thinks herself Valjean's daughter, misses only her doll, and runs to his hut for her hour each day. She laughs now. Her little mourning clothes lie locked in the scented valise by his bed. Years pass, and she grows up.

Thénardier's words in the Gorbeau garret make it plain: the girl Marius has worshipped at the Luxembourg, his 'Ursule', is the Lark of Montfermeil grown into a beauty, and her father is the man who carried her off. Thénardier means to hold her for ransom; her father's false address keeps her safe. Marius can only wonder whether she is the Lark.

Since 1829 she has lived with her father, M. Fauchelevent, in a hidden house in the Rue Plumet with a wild garden, served by a stammering maid, Toussaint. He took her out of the convent so that she could choose her own life rather than drift into the veil.

She left the convent at fourteen, plain, timid and ignorant of the world. She adores her father, prefers his bare lodge to her own tapestried drawing-room, and keeps only nightmare glimpses of the Thénardiers and of a night journey for water. She prays for a mother whose name she has never been told.

Overhearing Toussaint say how pretty she is growing, she looks in her mirror and dazzles herself. Within a month she has mastered bonnets and gowns and always wants to go out, while her father watches her beauty with dread.

Hugo retells the Luxembourg from her side: she had noticed the young man long before, steered her father toward his bench, and from the day their eyes met loved him without a word, not even knowing the name of what she felt.

When her father stops their walks she grows silent and pale. At the Barrière du Maine she watches the chain-gang pass and asks whether those are still men; days later she asks him what the galleys are like.
Nursing her father's burned arm for a month brings back their old closeness, and with the spring the shadow lifts from her.
Her grief fades so far that she begins to watch for a handsome lieutenant of lancers who passes the gate each day: Théodule Gillenormand.
A notebook of unsigned meditations on love, left under a stone on her garden bench, brings everything back. She knows at once who wrote it, and the lancer now looks hideous to her.
At dusk the young man is standing behind her in the garden. She faints into his arms, they kiss, and they talk for hours; only at the end do they exchange names: Marius, Cosette.

All through May he comes each night through a loose bar of the gate, and their love stays chaste to the point of innocence. She tells him her real name is Euphrasie, and decides she prefers Cosette because he does.
Her father tells her to be ready for a journey, perhaps to England, within a week. Marius swears on his honour that he will die if she goes, and scratches his address on the garden wall.

Moved that evening to the Rue de l'Homme Armé, she wrote Marius a few lines with her new address and gave them to a young workman at the gate to deliver. The young workman was Éponine, who kept the note until she lay dying at the barricade.

At dawn on 6 June she wakes sure that Marius has her letter and will come today. She knows nothing of the fighting, takes the cannon for carriage gates slamming, and watches a martins' nest below her window.
Months later her father brings her to the convalescent Marius's bedside. M. Gillenormand asks for her hand, and M. Fauchelevent announces that she has six hundred thousand francs.

On paper she becomes Euphrasie Fauchelevent, orphan of the 'other' Fauchelevent and heiress to an anonymous legacy. The grandfather showers her with heirlooms, and the aunt, won over by the money, decides to leave the couple her fortune.
She marries Marius on Shrove Tuesday, 16 February 1833, at the Gillenormand house and Saint-Paul, and Toussaint becomes her lady's maid.
Puzzled and hurt, she obeys her father's odd wish that she call him 'Monsieur Jean' and let him call her 'Madame', and, soothed by Marius, stops asking why.
Absorbed in her husband, she lets herself forget. She is told that Monsieur Jean has gone on a journey.

Marius tells her that the man who brought her up saved his life and gave her to him. They reach the Rue de l'Homme Armé in time: she scolds him for his cold hands, sits on his knee and kisses his brow, and hears at last that her mother was called Fantine. He dies with his hands on her head and Marius's.

description.text: For more than a year Marius has passed him on the same bench in the loneliest alley of the Luxembourg: about sixty, sad and serious, with the strong, weary look of a retired officer, very white hair, a blue coat, a broad-brimmed hat and a dazzling white shirt. He is always with a thin girl who seems to be his daughter, and gazes at her with great tenderness while she chatters. Courfeyrac named him Monsieur Leblanc for his hair; Marius has no other name for him, and likes him.

As Marius haunts the alley, the old gentleman seems to notice. He changes benches, sometimes walks about when Marius arrives, and sometimes comes alone. A handkerchief marked U. F. that Marius takes for the girl's was really his.

When Marius follows them home to the Rue de l'Ouest and questions the porter, M. Leblanc stops at his gate and stares hard at him. They do not come back to the Luxembourg, and a week later he has moved, leaving no address. The porter takes Marius for a police spy.
Months later, near the Invalides, Marius glimpses a man in workman's clothes with the same white hair and profile, only sadder, and loses him in the side streets. He decides it was a resemblance.

He turns out to be the 'benevolent gentleman' of the church of Saint-Jacques-du-Haut-Pas to whom the Jondrettes send a begging letter. He climbs to their garret with his daughter and a parcel of clothes and blankets, hears Jondrette's tale of ruin as the actor Fabantou, gives five francs, leaves his own greatcoat, and promises to come back at six with sixty francs for the rent. Jondrette studies him strangely throughout.

Once he has gone, Jondrette tells his wife he has recognised the man from eight years ago, whispers something about the young lady that sends her into a rage, and plans to have him at their mercy that evening. Marius still does not know who M. Leblanc is.

At six he comes alone and serene, lays four louis on the table for the rent and dismisses his cab. While Jondrette talks of a picture he must sell, silent men with blackened faces slip in behind him. When Leblanc values the daub at three francs, Jondrette drops his mask: 'Do you know me?'

tagline.text: A thin, plain girl of thirteen or fourteen who sits daily with M. Leblanc in the Luxembourg.
The same girl six months later, become a beautiful young woman.
The girl Marius is desperately in love with, without a word exchanged.
Vanished with her father, leaving Marius no address.
Found again by Marius through a hole in the wall, bringing charity to the Jondrettes.

description.text: When Marius first noticed her she was thirteen or fourteen, thin almost to plainness, awkward, in a badly cut black merino dress like a convent schoolgirl's, with a promise of fine eyes. She chatters to the white-haired man beside her, who looks like her father. Courfeyrac calls her Mademoiselle Lanoire; Marius finds her insipid.

After six months away from the alley Marius finds a tall, lovely girl of about fifteen beside the same man: brown hair threaded with gold, a marble brow, long chestnut lashes. The child has flowered. She glances at him with indifference.

Their eyes meet one spring day, and soon she looks at him as she passes with a pensive sweetness that sets him on fire. For a month she answers his looks with hers while talking naturally to her father.
Marius finds a handkerchief marked U. F. on their bench, decides her name is Ursule, and worships it.

Marius follows her home to a modest house in the Rue de l'Ouest and questions the porter. She and her father stop coming to the Luxembourg, and a week later they have moved away without an address. Marius searches Paris for her through autumn and winter.
Through the hole in the wall of the Gorbeau garret Marius sees her again, come with M. Leblanc to bring clothes and blankets to the starving Jondrettes.
When Jondrette pinches his younger daughter's cut hand to make her shriek, the young lady hurries to comfort her.
Marius, left with sixteen sous after giving his last five francs away, cannot pay a cab to follow her home.
Once she has gone, Jondrette whispers something about her to his wife that throws the woman into a jealous fury at the girl's fine clothes. Marius still does not know who she is.

moments.text: Noticed by Marius on a Luxembourg bench beside M. Leblanc.

tagline.text: A little Savoyard whose forty-sou piece Jean Valjean put his foot on.
The child whose stolen coin makes Jean Valjean a second offender.
The boy whose robbery sent Jean Valjean back to the galleys for life.

description.text: A Savoyard of about ten with a hurdy-gurdy and a marmot box, who comes singing along a path on the plain outside Digne at sunset, tossing his few coins. When a forty-sou piece rolls to the convict sitting behind a bush, Valjean sets his foot on it. The boy asks politely for his money, gives his name, pleads and cries, and runs off in terror when the man reaches for his stick. Valjean sees what he has done only after the boy is gone, and shouts 'Little Gervais!' across the empty plain in vain.

The theft of his forty sous is what makes Valjean a repeat offender, liable to the galleys for life if he gives himself up. The coin itself has stayed with Valjean; on the night of the Champmathieu affair it glints among the ashes of his burned clothes.
At the Arras Assizes Valjean names him: he robbed the Bishop and he robbed Little Gervais, and the coin lies among the ashes of his fireplace.
Before fleeing Montreuil-sur-Mer, Valjean leaves the blackened coin on his table with a label saying it is the forty sous stolen from Little Gervais.

Retaken in 1823, Valjean is tried at the Var Assizes for highway robbery with violence on a little Savoyard eight years before, condemned to death, and sent to the galleys for life when the King commutes the sentence.

moments.text: Robbed of his forty-sou piece by Jean Valjean on the plain outside Digne.
Named by Valjean in court as one of his victims.
His robbery cost Valjean a life sentence.

tagline.text: The elderly, stammering maid of the house in the Rue Plumet.
The incurious maid who follows her master to the Rue de l'Homme Armé.
Cosette's lady's maid in the Gillenormand house.
Gone from the Gillenormand house after quarrelling with Nicolette.

description.text: Jean Valjean saved her from the hospital and from wretchedness, and chose her for three qualities: she is elderly, from the provinces, and a stammerer. She is the only servant of the hidden house in the Rue Plumet. She and Cosette live in the pavilion. She was told that the young lady is mistress of the house and that monsieur is something better than the master: the father.
When her butcher calls M. Fauchelevent a queer fish, she answers that he is a saint.
It is her remark to Valjean in the garden, that Cosette is growing pretty, that sends Cosette running to her mirror.

Asked whether the shutters are barred at night, she says she fastens them like a prison, then terrifies Cosette with talk of men who come in at night to cut lone women's throats. Hugo asks leave not to transcribe her stammer any further.
She sleeps early and knows nothing of Marius's nightly visits. The burglars at the gate see only her light in the attic as she hangs linen to dry.

She goes with Valjean and Cosette to the Rue de l'Homme Armé without curiosity, 'I do my work; the rest is no affair of mine', and stammers out the news that there is fighting in Paris, toward Saint-Merry. A National Guard uniform has been glimpsed among her packages.
She admires the two silver candlesticks when they reappear on Valjean's chimneypiece.
She passes to Cosette as lady's maid and dresses her for her wedding.
She assures the Gillenormands that monsieur has always been like that, but she cannot get on with their servant Nicolette, and leaves.

moments.text: Told Valjean that Cosette was growing pretty, in Cosette's hearing.

The Waterloo prowler who robbed a wounded officer and was thanked as his rescuer.
Innkeeper, swindler and scientific thief, who rules his huge wife with a look.
The man who sold Cosette to a stranger for fifteen hundred francs.
The 'sergeant who saved my life' commended to Marius in his father's last note.

The blackmailer who came to damn Jean Valjean and proved him a hero.

description.text: In spring 1818 he is a man's voice from inside a failing cook-shop at Montfermeil, the Sergeant of Waterloo, when Fantine asks his wife to keep Cosette. He fixes the terms: seven francs a month, six months in advance, fifteen more for expenses. The money will cover a note due tomorrow; his daughters on the swing, he tells his wife, made a good mousetrap.

Hugo sketches him: one of a bastard class of coarse people who have risen a little and clever ones who have sunk, shadowy behind and threatening in front. He claims to have been a sergeant in 1815 and painted his inn sign himself to commemorate a feat of arms. The narrator reserves judgement on how much of it is true.

Once Fantine's money is gone he pawns the child's clothes and keeps raising the price, from seven francs to twelve, then to fifteen with a threat to send the child back once he learns she is illegitimate.

His letters to Montreuil-sur-Mer say Cosette is naked in the cold, then dying of a fever. Both are lies; Fantine sells her hair and then her front teeth to pay, and a last demand for a hundred francs drives her onto the streets.

When the mayor of Montreuil-sur-Mer sends three hundred francs and then three hundred more to bring Cosette to her mother, Thénardier scents a milch cow, invents bills for the child's illnesses, and keeps her.

On the night after Waterloo a prowler with a sutler's cart nearby strips the dead in the sunken road. Taking a buried cuirassier officer's ring, cross, watch and purse, he drags the man alive from under the corpses, and the officer, believing himself rescued, asks his name: 'Thénardier.' The officer's is Pontmercy.
In his tavern he and the schoolmaster ply the road-mender Boulatruelle with wine to learn what he has been digging for in the forest. Thénardier suspects something more solid than the devil's gold.

About fifty now, small, thin and sickly-looking but perfectly healthy, he smiles as a precaution, drops the names of Voltaire and Saint Augustine, and is a thief with a system. His tavern is named for the wounded general he claims to have carried out of the grapeshot at Waterloo; in fact he was one of the marauding sutlers who follow armies, and his capital came from the pockets of the dead. His giant wife seems the master, but he rules her with a word. In 1823 he owes fifteen hundred francs.

He takes the shabby stranger who arrives on Christmas Eve for a beggar and bills him twenty-three francs. When the man offers to take Cosette away, he protests that he adores the child, then names his price, fifteen hundred francs, and the stranger lays it on the table.

Stung by his wife's 'Is that all?', he runs after the pair to squeeze out more. The stranger shows a note in Fantine's hand ordering the child given to the bearer, reckons that Thénardier has already been overpaid, and sends him home with a look.
When the police come asking about the child taken from Montfermeil, he silences his wife, wary of drawing the law's eye to his own affairs, and describes a respectable 'grandfather'.

Colonel Pontmercy's last note asks his son Marius to do all the good he can to a sergeant named Thénardier who saved his life at Waterloo and now keeps an inn near Paris. Marius believes it; the reader knows what happened in the sunken road.

When Marius goes to Montfermeil to find him, the inn has failed and closed and no one knows where Thénardier has gone. For three years Marius has searched the villages for him in vain, and venerates his name beside his father's.

Jondrette, the begging-letter writer of the Gorbeau house, is Thénardier: he says so himself in his own trap. Since the inn failed he has lived in Paris under false names, Jondrette, Fabantou, Genflot, Don Alvarès, writing to the charitable and sending his daughters out with the letters. In the white-haired philanthropist he has recognised the man who carried off the Lark on Christmas Eve 1823, and with the Patron-Minette gang he means to extort two hundred thousand francs from him, with a red-hot chisel ready. The 'picture by a master' he offers for sale is his old inn sign. Behind the wall, Marius hears the name his father bequeathed him and cannot bring himself to fire.
Javert walks in. Thénardier's pistol misfires in his face, his wife hurls a paving-stone, and the whole gang is taken, while their victim slips out of the window.
He is in La Force, his wife at Saint-Lazare, his daughters at the Madelonettes. Every Monday Marius sends him five borrowed francs.

The narrator adds what became of the two sons born after 1823: the couple leased them to the woman Magnon in place of her own dead boys, so that M. Gillenormand would keep paying for them, and Thénardier drew ten francs a month for the loan. It was then that he became Jondrette.

On a stormy night he breaks out of the top-floor cages of La Force but is stranded on a ruined wall above the street, his rope too short. Montparnasse fetches Gavroche, who recognises his father and climbs a flue to tie the rope. Safe in the street, Thénardier asks only whom they are going to rob next, and never once turns toward the boy.

On 3 June he leads five of Patron-Minette to rob the house in the Rue Plumet. Éponine bars the gate and threatens to scream for the police, starting with her father; to his plea that they must eat she answers 'Burst!' The gang withdraws on Brujon's bad omens.

On 6 June he is hiding in the Grand Sewer with a key to the river outlet, a police agent waiting outside. When a mud-caked man arrives carrying a body, he does not recognise Jean Valjean, takes him for a murderer, pockets his thirty francs, tears a strip from the dead man's coat, and lets him out to throw his pursuer off his own trail.
The pursuer he dodged was Javert.

His wife has died in prison awaiting trial. As ringleader of the Gorbeau ambush he has been condemned to death in his absence, and he has sunk out of sight with Azelma; Marius's agents cannot find him.
On the wedding day, masked as an old Spaniard on a carnival cart, he recognises the old man with his arm in a sling in the bride's carriage and orders Azelma to find out where the wedding is going.

Disguised in a hired diplomat's suit, he calls on Marius as 'Thénard' to sell him the secret that Jean Valjean is a thief and murderer, and proves the reverse: newspapers show Valjean was M. Madeleine and that Javert killed himself, and the strip of coat he tore in the sewer fits the bloodstained coat Marius flings on the floor. Marius pays him to disappear. Two days later he sails for America with Azelma and twenty thousand francs, and sets up there as a slave-dealer.
Dying, Valjean asks Cosette to forgive the Thénardiers.

tagline.text: The innkeeper's wife at Montfermeil, swinging her two little girls, who agrees to keep Cosette.
Cosette's tormentor, who adores her own daughters and hates the stranger's child.
A bearded giantess who does all the work and fears only her husband.
The Gorbeau garret's Madame Jondrette: Thénardier's wife and his accomplice in the trap.
Taken by Javert after hurling a paving-stone at him; in Saint-Lazare.
The mother who gave away her two youngest sons for money.
Dead in prison, awaiting trial.

description.text: Outside the cook-shop at Montfermeil she swings her two little girls in the loop of a cart chain, humming a romance. Sandy-complexioned, thin and angular, barely thirty, she has the look of a soldier's wife with a languishing air borrowed from novels. It is the sight of her happy daughters that makes Fantine beg her to keep Cosette.

Twelve or fifteen years younger than her husband, she is just literate enough to devour the cheap romances of the day: a Pamela, Hugo says, with a Megaera underneath. The novels gave her daughters their names, Éponine and Azelma.

She adores her own girls and therefore hates the stranger's child, who takes blows that might otherwise fall on them. She dresses Cosette in rags, feeds her under the table with the dog and cat, beats her, and has made her the household drudge before she is five.

Nearing forty, she has become a colossus of the fairground: tall, blond, red, fat and square, bearded, swearing splendidly, able to crack a nut with her fist. She does all the work with Cosette as her only servant, a mouse in the service of an elephant. Everyone takes her for the master, but she adores and fears her husband. Her mothering stops at her daughters and does not reach to boys.
On Christmas Eve she catches Cosette in a lie about the peddler's horse and sends her out into the black night with a bucket for water.
She takes the shabby stranger for a beggar, reaches for the whip over Cosette's lost coin, and seethes when he buys the girl her freedom to play and the great doll from the stall.
She is delighted to be rid of Cosette until she sees what the stranger paid. Her 'Is that all?' sends her husband running after them.

Madame Jondrette, the huge wife crouched by the dead fire of the Gorbeau garret, is Madame Thénardier. When her husband recognised the charitable young lady as 'that beggar brat' of Montfermeil she raged at the girl's fine clothes while her own daughters went barefoot. In the trap she winds her hands in the prisoner's hair, carries his letter to a false address, and comes back furious at being duped, ready to cut his throat.

When Javert appears she shields her husband with her shawl and lifts a huge paving-stone over her head like a giantess. Javert ducks it and takes her by the shoulder. Handcuffed, she weeps for her daughters.
She is in Saint-Lazare.

She had two more sons after 1823 and, a mother to her daughters only, detested Gavroche and cursed the little ones. While they were still small she handed them to the woman Magnon to pass for Magnon's own dead boys, so that M. Gillenormand's money would keep coming. She felt, or seemed to feel, one scruple that evening; her husband cauterised it.
She has died in prison before her trial.
